Jewish baby naming. The ceremonies that formally welcome a newborn into the Jewish community and assign a Hebrew name are crucial to Jewish identity. A Hebrew name is essential and is used for all religious purposes, including aliyahs to the Torah and in ketubah documents, the marriage contracts that come much later in life.

Boys typically receive their names at the brit milah, the circumcision ceremony, which takes place on the eighth day after birth. Girls are welcomed through simchat bat ceremonies, called the daughter's joy, held shortly after birth. These ceremonies vary widely across communities. Some families hold them in the synagogue during the Torah service, while others organize private home celebrations called zeved habat.

In traditional practice, a child is not called by their Hebrew name until the formal naming ceremony has taken place, emphasizing the ritual's significance. The Hebrew name often honors a deceased relative, following Ashkenazi tradition, or reflects the family's hopes and connection to Jewish heritage. In many cases, the naming is announced during synagogue services, giving the broader community knowledge of the child's Jewish identity.

Modern Jewish movements offer diverse approaches to naming. Reform temples may hold formal naming ceremonies for any baby, while Orthodox practice follows more gender-distinct traditions. Following the naming ceremony, a festive meal called a seudah celebrates the child's welcome into the covenant community, bringing the extended family together to mark this milestone.

The Hebrew name connects the child to their heritage and to the community at a spiritual level that goes beyond the secular name given at birth. It is the name by which the child will be called when they are called to the Torah, whether at their bar or bat mitzvah years later or at other significant moments in their Jewish life.
